thread.title: UPDATE: Will TV's recent reboot trend tarnish its golden era?

author: morningstar.com
title: UPDATE: Will TV's recent reboot trend tarnish its golden era?
text:
By Trey Williams, MarketWatch
Disney CEO Bob Iger said the company is developing a few 'Star Wars' TV series for its forthcoming streaming service
TV has been on a reboot bender of late, with announcement after announcement from networks that they are bringing back beloved series from the past.
Networks have also taken risks and created some of the most creatively inspired and high-quality work on TV in years -- shows such as "Atlanta," "Game of Thrones" and "The Good Place" -- leading critics to talk of a "Golden Age" of TV. But at the same time, traditional networks have started mimicking film studios and are churning out familiar content to try to catch audiences' attention.
The CW, owned by Time Warner Inc. (TWX) and CBS Corp. (CBSA), said last month that it would reboot "Charmed," the Warner Bros. show about a trio of sisters who are powerful witches that first aired in 1998. The show starred Shannen Doherty, Holly Marie Combs, Alyssa Milano and later Rose McGowan.
Combs has been vocal on Twitter criticizing the plan to revive the series.
(https://twitter.com/H_Combs/status/956781792517701633)
CBS has announced plans to reboot "Murphy Brown," Walt Disney Co.'s (DIS) ABC is bringing back "Roseanne" and Comcast Corp.-owned (CMCSA) NBC is reviving "The Office."
Check out:'Roseanne' is coming back to TV -- how American families have changed since 1988 (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/roseanne-is-coming-back-to-tv-how-american-families-have-changed-since-1988-2017-05-18)
Then there's "Will & Grace" already airing again on NBC, "MacGyver" on CBS and 21st Century Fox Inc.'s (FOX) broadcast network brought back "The X-Files."
Media analyst Barton Crockett notes that tapping into popular old TV shows is a practice that Netflix Inc. (NFLX) has used for years, as it built up its original content library. The streaming giant has revived "Arrested Development," "Full House" and recently brought back "Queer Eye for the Straight Guy," to name a few.
"Success begets copy cats. Netflix has seemingly been pretty successful doing this" said Crockett, an analyst at B. Riley FBR.
The recent surge in TV reboots has drawn some backlash from audiences (http://tvline.com/2018/01/29/tv-reboot-trend-remakes-charmed-magnum-pi-murphy-brown-cagney-lacey/), who are questioning whether TV executives, like studio execs, have run out of ideas.
But it's not so much about an idea well drying up -- the number of scripted TV shows rose to 487 in 2017 (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/the-number-of-shows-on-tv-continues-to-rise-2018-01-05), up from 455 in 2016. The issue facing networks, rather, is the increased competition from new streaming platforms.
See:Most people aren't willing to spend more than $20 on streaming services (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/most-people-arent-willing-to-spend-more-than-20-on-streaming-services-2018-01-30)
Also read:Hollywood is still keeping black creators out of TV writers' rooms (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/hollywood-still-keeping-black-creators-out-of-tv-writers-rooms-2017-11-01)
"TV's not running out of ideas. But because the audience is so overwhelmed with choice, one way that networks -- the traditional broadcast networks in particular -- attempt to cut through the clutter is with familiar brand names," said Alan Sepinwall, TV critic and author of "TV (The Book): Two Experts Pick the Greatest American Shows of All Time."
"It's a lot easier to grab someone's attention by saying, "Will & Grace' is back!' than by saying, 'Here's a show that in certain ways might remind you of how you once felt about 'Will & Grace.'"
The recent surge in demand from services like Netflix, Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN), Hulu, and the CBS All Access's of the world for content has forced networks to leave no stone unturned. Things are bound to get more desperate as Apple Inc. (AAPL) and Facebook Inc. (FB) toss their deep pocketbooks into the ring.
Networks have also looked to tested intellectual property with built-in fan bases to mine new TV series. On Disney's most recent quarterly conference call, Chief Executive Bob Iger said the company is in the process of developing a few "Star Wars" series for its upcoming streaming service.
In 2015 CBS said it would make "Star Trek: Discovery," now streaming on CBS All Access, and Amazon paid a reported $250 million last year for the rights to make a "Lord of the Rings" TV show.
Read:Can 'Star Trek: Discovery' help make CBS's stand-alone streaming pursuit successful? (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/can-star-trek-discovery-help-make-cbss-stand-alone-streaming-pursuit-successful-2017-10-04)
In Hollywood this model has worked to varying degrees of success. On one side are the likes of Disney and its plans for live-action remakes of some of its most popular films. Last year's "Beauty and the Beast" was the second highest-grossing film of 2017, and 2016's "The Jungle Book" grossed $966.6 million worldwide and was well received by critics.
The past couple of years have also seen moviegoers reject the Hollywood cycle of reboots, franchises and remakes. The quality of some of these films, like "Ben-Hur" in 2016 and "Baywatch" last year, coupled with audiences' indifference, led to the overall box office underperforming.
Don't miss:Hollywood is running out of hit '80s movies to reboot (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/hollywood-loves-the-1980s-as-much-as-it-loves-franchises-and-remakes-2017-05-26)
Also see:Money talks, and its saying moviegoers are tired of Hollywood sequels (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/money-talks-and-its-saying-moviegoers-are-tired-of-hollywood-sequels-2016-06-03)
The fragmented TV landscape may help audiences overlook the reboot trend.
"There are so many more shows available all over the place that are original titles, whereas the way the movie business runs, your local theater might only have remakes and sequels some weeks," Sepinwall said. "Most of these [TV] remakes and revivals haven't worked, but enough of them have that we're going to keep getting them."
-Trey Williams;
